title: Roll back a bad deployment
applies_when: error rate or latency rose sharply within minutes of a deployment of the affected service, and the errors point to code introduced by the new release
steps: Confirm a deployment of the affected service happened shortly before the alert
Identify the previous known good version
Roll the service back to that version
Re-check the error rate after the rollback
cautions: Do not roll back if the release included a database migration that is not backward compatible; escalate instead. Needs human approval.

title: Clean up old logs on a full log volume
applies_when: disk usage on a log host is high and rising, log rotation is failing with no space left on device, and there was no recent deployment
steps: Confirm the volume holds logs and that rotation has been failing
Delete only archived or rotated logs older than the retention period
Never delete the active log files
Re-check disk usage after the cleanup
cautions: Only paths under /var/log may be cleaned. If usage does not fall below 80 percent, escalate because old logs may not be the cause.

title: Restart a leaking service
applies_when: memory use grows steadily for hours with no matching traffic increase, instances are killed for running out of memory, and latency spikes before each restart
steps: Confirm the memory trend is steady growth and not a traffic spike
Restart the instances one at a time
Watch the error rate while instances come back
Open a follow-up task to fix the leak
cautions: A restart briefly reduces capacity, so avoid it at peak traffic without approval. A restart clears the symptom, not the cause. Needs human approval.

title: Scale up a saturated service
applies_when: CPU is saturated on all instances, request volume is far above normal, latency is rising gradually, and there was no recent deployment
steps: Confirm the load is real traffic and not an error loop
Add instances in small increments
Watch latency and the error rate after each increment
Lower the autoscaling thresholds afterwards
cautions: Never scale above the platform limit of 20 replicas. Scaling a service that is failing for another reason wastes money and hides the cause. Needs human approval.

title: Flush a stale cache
applies_when: customers see outdated data, there are no errors and no deployment, but a bulk data import or update ran recently
steps: Confirm the cached entries predate the data import
Flush the cache for the affected service
Expect a short extra load on the database
Confirm fresh data is now served
cautions: Flushing during peak load can overload the database. There is no automated verification for this action, so a human must confirm the result.

title: Escalate to the on-call engineer
applies_when: the cause appears to be outside our systems such as a third-party outage, the evidence conflicts, confidence is low, or no other runbook fits
steps: Page the on-call engineer with the incident summary and the evidence gathered
Do not change any infrastructure
Record what was checked so the engineer does not repeat it
cautions: Prefer escalation over a guess when confidence is low or a caution in another runbook applies.
